utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone, and this being the first session since we formally adjourned before the break, I wish everyone a happy new year. I heard the tail end of a news item this morning which I may have gotten out of context but something to the effect that productivity is higher in countries with colder climates, so to the extent that there's any validity to that observation, the experience that you would have had in these parts over the past three weeks has meant that you are all well invigorated and ready for a productive next few months. So the -- I believe where we were at the adjournment is that the witness Donia was on the stand being cross-examined. And unless there are any other matters which would -- which need engage our attention, we would resume at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well good morning, Your Honours, and happy new year to you from the Prosecution. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, assisted by Case Manager, Crispian Smith. I just have one gentle inquiry for the new year, whether we are going to get any decisions in the very, very, very immediate future?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You said very, very immediate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, like, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The decisions are in progress, and you will receive them shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just then mention for the purposes of the record, that one of the decisions relates to the witness who is supposed to be coming tomorrow. Or may have an effect, can I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we haven't lost sight of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Happy new year to you too. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Tatjana Savic appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. However, Mr. Cvijetic who is conducting the cross-examination of witness Donia has one preliminary matter he would like to raise with Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic, could we have the appearances for the Zupljanin, please, and then we will hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. At the same time I would like to express a deepest condolences for the loss of UN officials in the Haiti earthquake tragedy, as well as the number of people of Haiti, but the same time we were informed that the Serbian police officers members of UN staff at Haiti are well and they are doing best in their recovery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I waited for the interpretation to end. I also wish you a happy new year. As my colleague Mr. Zecevic has said, I cross-examined Mr. Donia, and we broke off when we discussed a topic with which I would like to resume today. Mr. Pantelic and I redistributed the topics we will deal with, and we made a time estimate in view of finishing with Mr. Donia today. One of our conclusions which we are certain about is that we will finish our cross-examination of Mr. Donia today. Only we are not sure how much time will be used by either of us. But we would like to ask you to allow Mr. Pantelic and me to work with Mr. Donia during three sessions. So far we haven't been able to prepare a video-clip we would like to show, and we will continue preparing it to be shown during the first session, and we would like to show it during the second session during which I would like to finish with Mr. Donia, and Mr. Pantelic will take over, so, so much for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I understand, Mr. Cvijetic, correctly, this video on which they are still working, in which -- in respect to which I gather there are certain technical problems; however that is -- while that is being worked through, the bottom line is that the witness Donia must be concluded today including re-examination by the Prosecution. So we would begin immediately with the cross-examination, and see -- to maximise the time that we have. Maximise use of the time that we have. And the -- such work as has to be done on this video that you wish to use would continue. Could the usher have the witness return to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia, I remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have the English versions of both publications of Mr. Donia. I can see that Mr. Donia doesn't have any copies on him, so I would like to ask the usher to pass this to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And a happy new year. Can we start? Mr. Donia, I'm going to remind you briefly that last time we started dealing with a topic we couldn't finish. I tried to introduce a Defence document which was a letter written by the parents of Muslim children from Neum in which they asked for instructions from the headquarters of the SDA party in Sarajevo as to what they should do because they were required to send their children to school where they would be taught from school books from Croatia. This letter is dated 16 September 1991. You said that this letter might not be relevant for this trial because, according to you, the Croatian community of Herceg Bosnia was established later that is in November 1992, that's what you said to the transcript. And in your work - and we are now on page 32 of the B/C/S version, and it's page 34 of the English version - you state that the exact date is the 18th of November, 1992. I would like to go into that a bit deeper because the Trial Chamber was reluctant to accept my document until we clarify the date issue and the things related to the existence of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I ask Exhibit 1D00-3678 to be displayed. I apologise, but we have a binder with exhibits for Mr. Donia so he doesn't have to read off the screen. Could I ask the usher to pass it on to the witness, please. To speed up things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, the exhibit that can be seen on the screen is under tab 8 in this binder. This is an accompanying letter drafted by Mr. Mate Boban in which he addresses the president of the Republic of Croatia personally. The letter was sent to Zagreb. And Mr. Boban informs him of the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg Bosnia. Number 8 it was. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On the following page, as an enclosure to this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the following page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is the decision about the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg Bosnia. We can see it on the screen. You can also find it on the following page. Have you found it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this decision. You know it. Well, my question is very simple, when you said that the Croatian community of Herceg Bosnia was established on the 18th of November, you were probably referring to this decision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And you recognise it, we needn't read it and comment it. I will simply ask to tender this into evidence as this is a document recognised by you and which you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask that this document be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we now please see Exhibit 1D00-3672.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's under tab 9, Dr. Donia, you have probably found it already.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only for the benefit of the Bench we will say what it is; it's a statutory decision that accompanies the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is whether this statutory decision point toward a high degree of statehood attributes of the HZ HB due to the content of this statutory decision?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it attributes some degree of statehood to that, about the same as, say, the decision on the formation of the community of municipalities of Bosnia and Krajina. Less, far less than full statehood, but some attributes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. The point of my question was exactly the existence of some attributes of statehood, I didn't mean that there was full statehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this into evidence. Also since the witness obviously is familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may have noticed some hesitation when you asked to tender the last document, and I wonder -- I would now raise the question that I thought of, whether these don't fall into that package of documents to which we had referred about in November or thereabouts which are being statutory or quasi-statutory, didn't have to be formally exhibited but would form part of a list to be sorted out at some point between the sides - what do you call it, the law library, yes, called the law library - or whether this isn't a part of that -- wouldn't be a part of that package.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. No. I believe that the Prosecutor will also agree. That package of ours includes regulations and laws at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are regulations that apply only to a smaller area, and they will be used only when mention is made of the Croatian committee of Herzegovina Bosna, that's why I seek to tender it now without waiting to for the entire package.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only query I have, Your Honour, is why this is relevant, that's all. That's the only query, not -- it's certainly not part of the package of laws. But I don't understand on what basis it's said to be relevant to the community of Herceg Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, that did occur to me, Ms. Korner, but the question, the last question that was put to the witness, I see the context for it, the last exchange question and answer to the witness, his observations, his comments on the effect of this. So to that extent it would be admissible, would be relevant and therefore admissible. So it is admitted and marked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we will now return to the point the Defence wishes to make in connection with the letter which I don't want to put back on the screen right now. Instead I want to show Exhibit 1D00-3693. It's under tab 11 in your binder, Doctor. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, I can merely assist you, you may or may not know Smiljko Sagolj has signed as editor of the news programme of the Sarajevo TV. The content of this letter isn't very interesting to me, but what I am more interested in is the way Mr. Sagolj addresses Mr. Boban. It says, To Mr. Mate Boban, president of the HZ HB. And what is most interesting in all this is the date, in November 1990. Mr. Donia, after the multi-party elections in the field, the Croatian community Herceg Bosnia was in fact established, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, it was established formally on November 18, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I've just shown a document from which we can see that it is, in fact, functioning, and that it has had a president from 1990. Do you accept that this community was in fact in existence before it was officially established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- the English copy that I'm looking at has a question mark associated with 1990, I think suggesting that it may have been 1991. That would be the correct date of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you just take a look at the B/C/S version, the printed version. Do you have the B/C/S version? It's a fax with the date.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it says 1990, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. But despite that, you quite obviously don't agree with the point I'm making that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna existed since 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I don't agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let me go back to your report, the one you prepared for the Karadzic trial, and let me just remind you, I think you say there that the Croatian Defence Council as an armed formation of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was established, unless I'm very much mistaken, in April 1992. Do you remember your paper on that? I think you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, just a moment, please. May I just take a moment to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you remember saying that, do you not? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That it was in April?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think I've found the footnote, just to tell Ms. Korner. I apologise, I just have to take a moment. The Croatian Defence Council was established on the 8th of April, 1992, by the president of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and that is in footnote 118 in that additional paper, and it's to be found on page 41 of the B/C/S, but I'm sure you'll be able to find it if you look at the footnote 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found that, Doctor -- well, you know it anyway because you wrote it; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it, and I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just please pause for a moment. Can you tell me what you are describing as the Karadzic reports? The only two reports which have been exhibited in this case are the origins of the Republika Srpska and the Bosnian Krajina. Now, what is the Karadzic report? Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ms. Korner seems to have forgotten that part of that paper has been admitted into evidence in our case, and that's the portion that I'm referring to, the one deemed relevant by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- Mr. Cvijetic is absolutely right. I call it the Sarajevo report, and that's why I got slightly confused as to what the Karadzic report was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, linked to that particular date, may we have document 1D00-3853 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Cvijetic, but Ms. Pidwell reminds me, you only admitted chapters 4 to 6. What Mr. Cvijetic has just referred to is outside that. Now, I don't mind, I wanted the whole report in anyhow, but it's going to make it a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four, five, and six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the reference -- the citation which Mr. Cvijetic is made is in fact within what we have ruled as admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows one should always double-check information. Your Honour is right. I'm sorry, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you have the exhibit in the binder under number 10, so could you take a look at Exhibit number 10, please, Mr. Donia. There you will be able to see a letter from the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna on a letterhead of the Croatian Defence Council on their paper. The text isn't too relevant. What is relevant is the date. It's the 1st of June, 1990. Now, Mr. Donia, whichever way you look at it, both the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and this armed section of its army were established in 1990, and that is confirmed by this document; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't see a date on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S version on the screen, you'll see a date, I believe, there. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It says the 1st of June, 1990. So I asked you the question, and it was as follows: From these two documents can we see that we have an entity on the ground as early as 1990, a Croatian entity, that is, with it's armed formation as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think you are looking at the dates that are coming from the fax heading, and both of them have the characteristic of a date that -- to which there is no relationship to the document. The document in both of these cases would not make sense to have taken place well before the elections of November 18, 1990. I believe it's most likely that this is simply a fax machine header that someone forgot to set the correct date to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll just say briefly that it seems quite improbable that on the documents that the HZ HB and the Croatian Defence Council wasn't working properly and that this was somebody doing it retroactively, but I'll leave that to the Trial Chamber to assess the authenticity of the document. And I will now move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic, for my own edification, do I -- I'm trying to phrase this carefully because since you can't give evidence, do I understand the position to be that in the original B/C/S version, the date nowhere appears? And yet your question was based only on the date in the fax header? So the date, in fact, is not there, in the B/C/S version; is that the position? Is it in the body, or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, just looking at the upper date when the fax was sent, I'm making the conclusion that it is 1990. That's the only piece of evidence that I'm able to conclude this on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, let's now move into 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that let us look at document 1D00-3511.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's number 13 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it? Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The precedent document, are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, both the previous documents, I omitted to state that. There are two that I'd like it to tender, the letter by Smiljko Sagolj, the edited 1D3693 and 1D00-3853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 1D143, and 1D144 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents will become Exhibits 1D143 and 1D144.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this is the Official Gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, as you can see there in the heading. Document number 13 is what you should be looking at. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And here you have the regulations of the HZ HB that were published, and among others on the left-hand side you have the decree on the establishment of a division of the Supreme Court of the HZ HB. Can you see that decree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in Article 5 it says how the members are elected and relieved of duty, and that it is exclusively at the proposal of the Presidency or recommendation of the Presidency of the HZ HB. And then there's another decree that refers to the Prosecutor's Office. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, going on to the next page, because I have one question I need to ask you on the basis of all these four decrees, so let's look at the other two decrees, I think it's on the following page. We have already seen two, and now I'd like to look at two more. Next page, please. It is the application of the law on public law and order of Herceg-Bosna, and road safety, a decree on road safety. So those are two decrees on the implementation of the law of public law and order and road safety.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, I've asked you to look at those documents because I wanted to talk about a decree which says that the provisions and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be applied on the territory of Herceg-Bosna as well, that they should be applicable there too, only if they are not in contravention with these decreases and articles and some other regulations passed on the basis of these principle articles. So does that remind you of the attributes of statehood for HZ HB because it has an Official Gazette, it is publishing its own decrees and articles and selects the BH regulations that could be applicable and applied to the HZ HB? Is that the state attributes that you had in mind when you said that, yes, indeed, it did have certain attributes of statehood?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The attributes of statehood to which I referred in response to your earlier question were those in the decree of November 18, 1991, in particular the last three sections or sentences of that decree. These, to me, would go further in adding attributes of statehood to what was essentially an expanded concept of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, that's precisely my point. I think that if you look at the last decree there, that fines are paid in Croatian currency, the Croatian dinar, that's what it says there, is it not? Can you find that portion? It's in Article 2 of the decree on road safety. Can you see that, the portion about fines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So a currency is being produced that wasn't legal tender in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but was in Croatia; do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it wasn't legal tender in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know for sure that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But I assume you do know that it was a separate currency intended for HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Donia. We have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence. It is 1D00-3511. In view of the answers given by Mr. Donia, I think that they confirm the Prosecution [as interpreted] case on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Defence case on this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, admitted at Exhibit 1D145.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we have to move on. With the Dayton Peace Accords, and its general knowledge that the HZ HB by those accords was not recognized as a separate entity; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Similarly, the military formations were abolished and a joint Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military formations were not abolished, but there was a joint army of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant to say. Perhaps I didn't express myself properly, or it wasn't interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's look at the next document which is 1D00-4526.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's number 14 in your binder. Here we have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we zoom up so that we can see the title of the document. That's right. To show the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, unless I'm mistaken, we are dealing with December 1996 here and the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna still has its Official Gazette, and it's still called Herceg-Bosna, right, and here we have a decree, and I just selected one by way of an example. It's a decree having the force of law on amending the law governing the army of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, and it stipulates the ranks of the officers of the Croatian Defence Council. Can you find that? It's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How, then, can you explain this fact, Mr. Donia, the fact that in December 1996, that is to say one year after Dayton, the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, still exists, it has its Official Gazette, it publishes its regulations and decrees and even deals with its own armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was maintained illegally in violation of the Dayton Accords for some time after the signing of Dayton. It's less clear whether the HVO was in fact a legitimate part of the armed forces. There is, I believe, one provision in the Dayton constitution, or at least the military annex, that recognizes the HVO. But the HZ-- or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was clearly not a part of the Dayton Agreement, and it was eventually terminated, I believe, in 1998. But until that time it existed, it operated in contravention of the Dayton Agreement provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to smile, I don't know what is coming next. I think you are agreeing with me, so I'll continue along those lines not to upset the barrel. So that is the absence of it, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna did in fact continue to exist. And my next question, and that will round off this subject of Herceg-Bosna, we'll finish with that topic, but you were a system professor at the University of Sarajevo for time, were you not, and you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina frequently; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just in your transition to this new line, you made the statement that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna continued to exist. It did not. In 1993 the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was converted to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that is what existed from that time until 1998. I was and am an associate professor at the University of Sarajevo without pay, without work, but who in fact was given that title several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to give you my own impressions and try to see if you agree and whether you share my impressions. I travelled around -- well, let's call it the one-time Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna or the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, so when I go there, I have the same feeling -- I have the feeling that it still exists looking at the radio and television stations, the various headings that you see there, so have you travelled around the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you have that same feeling, that it still exists, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Obviously we don't share the same impressions. I have a different impression. Of course we needn't agree on that point. Very well. Now, Mr. Donia, let's move on to another area, and -- well, Your Honour, I apologise but I forgot to tender the Official Gazette of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna into evidence. We have had quite robust commentary from Mr. Donia. It's 1D00-4526.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This one I do object to, Your Honours. Absolutely nothing to do with this case at all. Miles out of the period, totally irrelevant to any issue that Your Honours may have to decide upon as to whether they tried continue in violation of the Dayton Agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to add to that there's no English translation in e-court. So Mr. Cvijetic, the document will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I will be abide by your decision, but the Registry has told me that we do have an English translation. If that's the reason for it not being admitted. But let me say by way of explanation, the document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that wasn't the reason, right. Yes, I accept your decision, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we are now on page 31 of your paper entitled "The Origins of Republika Srpska." Actually, in English it's pages 33 and 34, to help you find your way. And I'll prepare by questions while you are doing that. On that page, you deal with the question of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was held, as we know, on the 15th of October, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th to 15th October, 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at that same Assembly, a decision was made about the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. I think the Assembly passed a resolution about sovereignty, but it really didn't make a decision about it. It simply drew attention to the sovereignty that had already been expressed in one of the amendments to the constitution passed in July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you for that explanation. But at any rate, we are not challenging the fact that the resolution was adopted without the presence of the Serbian representatives in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina so it was only the Croats and Muslim deputies who voted for it, or the deputies representing the parties of the SDA and the HDZ; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At that Assembly, the Serbian deputies tried to prevent that kind of decision from going through, saying that it was unconstitutional, that it was violating the constitution because it touched upon the vital interests of one of the nations. Mr. Karadzic took the floor several times and tried to draw the Assembly's attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we now have Exhibit P13. Exhibit P13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's under tab 15, I forgot to point that out, sorry. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was only one in a series of appearances. I mentioned the page references in both versions, and it was a rather dramatic appearance and you also commented Mr. Izetbegovic's reaction who understood that to be a threat. And later only one sentence was singled out from that speech and which was characterised as a threat. But, Mr. Donia, I'll be brief about this because this document is already in evidence, and we have discussed it earlier. Wouldn't it be fair to read Mr. Karadzic's entire speech, and then draw the conclusion that essentially he is actually asking those present not to adopt such a decision which is unconstitutional. You also quoted one of -- one sentence on page 3 of the B/C/S version, a few lines down, it says, as his final argument, he says, "My gentlemen, until you -- this issue of the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina is taken off the agenda, I will continuously take the floor." He is threatening that he will use constitutional means to prevent some things that he -- to contact The Hague. And finally, in a dramatic matter, I agree, he warns of the possible consequences as have been seen in Croatia. Mr. Donia, do you agree with me when I say that this document must be interpreted in the context of his entire speech and not only with regard to a few singled out sentences?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I do. And I think it also should be taken in the context of other utterances that he made in the immediate several days preceding this one on the floor of the Assembly to understand what his -- what his statement really meant in the context that he was uttering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you will agree with me when I say that in that context we should -- in that context we should also interpret his subsequent behaviour because after that Assembly war did not break out, mediation ensued by the international community, and Mr. Karadzic agreed to a plan in which there was no Greater Serbia or truncated Yugoslavia, but rather a sovereign Bosnia. Isn't that the context in which we should view that speech of his?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't think that is the context in which to view it in the first instance in any case. The immediate context was that that very day, the 15th of October, marked, that evening, the beginning of a protracted planning process in which Dr. Karadzic and others undertook to lay plans for a separate Serb state within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, the Republika Srpska was not planned to be a separate Serbian state outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor was it envisaged such by the constitution of Republika Srpska. Therefore I must show you Exhibit P181.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see it on our screens, please. And in your binder, it's under page 17. That's the constitution, and if we could see Article 143 of the constitution. It's at the very end of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, something I don't understand really. You seem to talk about a separate Serbian state outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness -- the witness was talking about a separate Serb state within Bosnia. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I didn't understand the interpretation, it may have been my mistake, but I think it was interpreted that way. Well, we'll clarify based on this constitutional article. I heard it the other way around, but we can check it with the witness, Your Honour. Or let's hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you were interpreting Karadzic's -- Karadzic's aspirations with regard to the Republika Srpska, what exactly did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to his aspirations to create a separate Serb state within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well then, you are right, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now read Article 143. Have you reached the final provisions of the constitution yet, sir? Let us try to corroborate my case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 143 is what you -- I've' reached it. I read it. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you see, the constitution leaves open the possibility of being adapted to the constitutional acts of Bosnia-Herzegovina because negotiations about that were still underway, so the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still uncertain and open, which is reflected here. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at this time there was no constitutive act that I know of on the order of relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If there were, and, indeed there were, discussions going on both among the parties and with the international community about what those relations would be, and had they been successful, they might have resulted in such a constitutive act. But it didn't exist at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, we will get to those negotiations yet. But before the break, let me ask the following question about this Assembly. Actually we have only two questions about it. Can you agree with me, sir, that with this Assembly resolution, a serious constitutional and political crisis began in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that it was a watershed event, in that it sent the various parties heading in different directions. Arguably the constitutional crisis could be dated earlier than this, but it certainly intensified that crisis to the point of affecting the way in which the primary political parties behaved thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, and my second question about this decision is the following: I'm asking you to state your opinion, you don't need to be an expert for constitutional law, I believe, and so, therefore, I believe I may ask this question. Was this decision in the spirit of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question. It's clear that the various parties had very different understandings of what the constitution provided, and that in some cases, those understandings were not really based on an examination of the constitution as much as wishful thinking. But whether it was in accord with the constitution or even the spirit of the constitution, I really can't -- I'm not an expert in that area and really can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I noticed that for constitutional and other legal issues, you consulted certain works of literature, you indicated as much in the footnotes. And several times you consulted Mr. Robert Hayden's book, a draft for a divided house, or some such. Am I correct when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of the things I examined, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this may be a good opportunity for us to take a look at Defence Exhibit 1D01-1156.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's under tab 16, Doctor. It's an excerpt from a Mr. Robert Hayden's book "Blueprints For a House Divided." Could you please turn to page 94. Not page 94 of the document, but that page of the book. It's in the second sheet in your binder, Doctor, I believe. So I would now like to ask you to skim through it to see what Mr. Hayden says about this decision.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It would seem that his position is that such a decision was not in line with the spirit of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree with Mr. Hayden's comment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Because he fails here to note the -- I believe he fails here, if I'm reading the context correctly, that he fails to note that the -- there was an effort it to create a council of national equality, not as a separate Chamber of legislature, but as a kind of committee drawing members from both other chambers -- both chambers of the legislature. And the legislature, or the Assembly failed to adopt -- failed to appoint the members to that, failed to adopt a working document which would form it. And the absence of that body, to me, was a crucial step in understanding what happened on the 15th of October, why the -- Dr. Karadzic and the SDS was so adamantly opposed to the vote or to the propositions that were submitted, and also why the HDZ and SDA felt comfortable in moving forward and voting for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe that we agree with Mr. Hayden that there was no constitutional mechanism for the protection of vital national interest because in the Assembly there was no house of peoples, and of course that council wasn't established or did it ever meet. Essentially, that is in line with what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the period before the elections, all three nationalist parties agreed that there should be, A, either third chamber; or a body such as the council of nationalities to ensure the protection of rights of each nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but nothing of the kind was in existence, was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provision for it was in existence in the constitution, but it was never actualised by an act of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my next topic is unrelated, so should we have a break now, or should I start dealing with this new topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, we are eight minutes away from the break, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I will now be dealing with a topic. Before we move on to Cutileiro's plan with which I'll finish, but until that time I'd like to dwell on a topic you are dealing with on pages 30 through 33 in the English version of your work, your basic paper. And it's pages 28 through 31 in the B/C/S. I want to go into the transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which one? Which report, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first report, the creation of Republika Srpska, the first basic report we are dealing with anyway. The page reference for the English version is 30 through 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you know what I'm referring to, the transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You are arguing that the Yugoslav People's Army started transforming into a Serbian military ever since Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, not a date. I mean, from the war in Croatia. I believe that I found that position expressed subsequently in your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that the war in Croatia really intensified to a full war sometime in September 1991, I would see the first indications of the transformation of the JNA in Bosnia as well, that it was a slow process that didn't gain momentum until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to show you some documents from an earlier period so that we may see whether such an attitude toward the JNA existed in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us see now a document number 1D00-3848. It's under tab 25 in your binder, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this document is unambiguously dated, it's 1991, and the Citluk municipality is in the area of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. With this decision they introduced a moratorium on sending recruits to the JNA, but this is mid-1991. You will certainly agree with me, sir, that the transformation of the JNA began, among other things, in such a way also.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the transformation of the JNA had several different components, and this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document because the witness appears to be in agreement with the allegations in this document and with the -- with the case of the Defence -- with the point of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, could we now see document 1D00-054 [as interpreted]. It's under tab 27, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us not comment, I'll just ask you whether you agree with me that here the HDZ BiH asks their members in 1991 to refrain from sending their children to the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. I would like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the following document is one by the SDA, let's see, its attitude towards the JNA. It's document 1D00-3840. Can we see it, please. It's under tab 26, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here the SDA, if you can see, is suggesting to prevent the taking over of documentation from the JNA to hide registers of possible recruits who could be drafted to the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see the word "hide" here unless we have a translation issue. It merely asks that the police be the guardians of those military records. That they be -- also be involved in guarding those records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But the purpose of this act is actually to prevent the JNA from laying their hands on these documents and gaining control over these documents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states that this recommendation or order is in response to those actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Since there seems to be a bit of controversy about this, could we take the break now and return to this in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is returning to the stand, we would alert counsel that we would need 10 minutes before the end of the -- today's adjournment to deal with a number of matters in which the Chamber will make some rulings. And I emphasise that the witness Donia, must be completed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we don't want to deal with this document very long so I will be specific. Please direct your attention to paragraph 2 where basically the republic is overruling the federal law on military service, and there is also another fact, namely that a political party is dealing with this matter rather than the political authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina because -- do you see the contradiction because these are matters with which the authorities of the republic or the Presidency can deal with, et cetera? Can we agree that this has a bearing on the functioning of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we, please, see a document from this group, 1D00 -- Your Honours, I have again forgotten, now the witness has agreed with my point, and therefore I seek to tender this document as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The final document is 1D00-3783. It's under tab 24, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the decision on the right side. It's the decision to withdraw representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina from all federal organisations. Twenty-four on the right-hand side, the upper decision. Well, maybe not in the English language version. Have you seen the decision on the withdrawal of representatives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It is short, and we won't comment much on it. It is dated the 25th of January, 1992. The vice-president of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of BiH, that is the Assembly function without the Serb's representatives, he assigned the decision to withdraw all representatives of the SR BiH from all federal bodies and organs. So my question is about the context of the relationship with the JNA. You will agree, won't you, that this obviously is the falling apart of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, what is it, according to you you, then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Be brief, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want ask me a question, I'll answer it as best I can. The withdrawal of representatives was -- put Bosnia in the same position as the other two western republics had earlier -- had taken earlier. It was not necessarily a permanent withdrawal insofar as it was prior to the referendum, certainly subject to being reversed, if the referendum result had gone in another direction, and so I wouldn't say this is the end of the Federation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that this is one in a series of actions and decisions that go in the direction of the deconstruction of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, in your report on the pages on which you deal with the JNA, you mentioned some incidents for which you blame JNA members. I believe there were shooting incidents in town caused by drunken soldiers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please call up -- I apologise, I forgot to seek to tender the previous document into evidence. I believe it isn't too late yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already an exhibit, 1D101 and 102. I think those were the numbers, or 1D102. 1D102 is the document number. It's an Exhibit, and Mr. Donia, it is under P19 in your set of documents. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have an additional act from Jelko Doko, the minister of national Defence, which is sending on the decision on the withdrawal of JNA units from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'd like us to have a look at the decision itself, now, please, because we see that the decision was attached to this document. It's on the next page. That's right, here it is. Mr. Donia, I assume that you know of this decision, you know that the Presidency took the decision to withdraw the JNA from BH and stipulated the conditions under which this should be done; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it's a document which is common knowledge. I have a few comments to make with respect to the documents that followed on from this decision, but this is already an exhibit and you know about the decision, so I think I can just move on to the next document. It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D00-2795 is the next document I'd like us to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, it is document number 20 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's just see if it's the right one. It was signed by Alija Delimustafic. Yes, right, that seems to be it. Mr. Delimustafic as minister of the interior is referring to the Presidency decision on the withdrawal of JNA units, and that's what it says in the introduction, before we come to the order itself. And under point 4, among other things, he says that planning should be accelerated and combat throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and that all this should be co-ordinated with the Territorial Defence, et cetera, et cetera. Now, Mr. Donia, my question to you linked to this order is this, the order from Mr. Delimustafic: Does this look to you like a declaration of war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next document, and then I'll tender both of them. It is an order from the commander of the Territorial Defence, the contents are the same. 1D00-2798 is the document I'd like us to look at next.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, it is document number 21 in your set.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's just wait for it to come up on our screens. The same heading again, it refers to the Presidency decision, and this time the order was signed by Colonel Hasan Efendic on behalf of the Territorial Defence staff, and in paragraph 4, the same thing is stated, that combat activities throughout the territory should be initiated, and it is symptomatic that this follows on from the decision taken by the Presidency about the withdrawal of the JNA, so once again I'm asking you, is this tantamount to a declaration of war against the JNA? And I assume that your answer will be the same as it was a moment ago, not to waste too much time on that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've asked the question a little bit differently this time. You said this time, is it tantamount to a declaration of war? And I would say it has some elements of a declaration of war, but as you know, that formal declaration did not -- did not really come about. So it's not a declaration of war, but has some elements of it. And in that context that the JNA was basically assaulting these forces all across the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, I can agree with you in part because you are coming close to my point, the point I want to make, but of course we don't have to agree 100 per cent. Anyway, I'd like to tender these two documents. They are historically important documents, in my view. So I'd like to tender them into evidence, and they are highly relevant for a clarification of the topic at hand. Do you wish me to repeat the numbers? 1D02795 and 2798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D150 and 1D151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, now, let's have Exhibit 1D00-3818 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, it's document number 22 in your set.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we move on to the second page straightaway, and I'll tell you what it's about. So page 2 of the document, please. This is the transcript from a Presidency meetings, Presidency session of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To be accurate, Your Honour, it's a newspaper publication of something said to be a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the transcript of the meeting that was published in the press because the press had a series of articles publishing transcripts from Assembly sessions, and I set aside this particular one which is relevant for my questions, but, yes, Ms. Korner is right. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And can you focus on the comment made by Mr. Delimustafic there. It starts with the following words: "Both we and his ministry made mistakes..." And then he goes on to comment and say that instead of him, the order to attack the JNA was signed by Mr. Avdo Hebib his assistant. And he goes on to stay when he ordered the war to start, people would open fire and occupy the barracks. And Mr. Izetbegovic asks, Who did that? And Delimustafic says, Avdo Hebib. And Delimustafic says, He declared war on the army. And after that a Croatian Presidency member asked that this should not be recorded and become part of record, but it was recorded and it did become part of the record. Now, my question to you is this: Do you still stand by your statement that this wasn't de facto a declaration of war against the JNA, I'm not talking about informal terms, but de facto? And Delimustafic referred to it in that same way.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I hold my earlier answer. There's no date here assigned to this alleged declaration, and the characterisation is given by Delimustafic who obviously was unhappy with what Hebib did. So I don't know that it's a very authoritative description.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, it means what Delimustafic says, I don't want to paraphrase what he says, he says himself that this is a declaration of war on the Yugoslav army. But anyway, if you have no further comments, then since this is a very important and historical document, I'd like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Donia -- yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Donia, the last document linked to this transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army is 1D19, it's already an exhibit so I don't need to tender it, but I'd just like us to comment on it. 1D19 is the number. It's document number 23, Mr. Donia, in your set. As you can see there, and the Trial Chamber has already seen this document, it's an exhibit, perhaps you haven't, but it is a chronology of important events, and it lists the incidents and attacks against members of the Yugoslav People's Army conclusive with the 30th of May. And it lists all the key incidents where a lot of members of the Yugoslav People's Army fell casualty, the attack in Sarajevo, Tuzla, the victims were in their hundreds, and so on. Mr. Donia, could this be the result of that declaration of war from that decision we saw earlier on, at least the events that took place after the decision?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't had a chance to review all of these. Clearly many of them are prior to the decision, and I couldn't -- I also don't know what the source of this document is. I just comment that many of them are prior to the decision and many are after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we know what the source was, please? Is?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we admitted this document, I think that a military person told us that it was -- that the source was military intelligence. No, I apologise, it was just marked for identification. Not admitted into evidence. So you are quite right, and we'll wait for a more opportune moment, I won't be tendering it now, but we'll wait for an expert to come in, so I withdraw that proposal to tender the document, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but I'm sorry, Dr. Donia has asked what the source is, and I'm repeating that request on behalf of the Prosecution. What is the source of the document, whether or not it's tendered? It's been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already answered that. I said that I think we had a military expert here, I can't remember his name, or a military person, and he confirmed that it was most probably from the military intelligence service, and that is why it was not tendered into evidence and admitted before we have an authentic explanation for the document's source. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, that is a misunderstanding. I want to know from where it was obtained? Who provided it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we obtained this document from the government commission or Secretariat dealing with war crimes in BH. A member of that commission. He was a Defence witness. He is a Defence witness, and we are going to try and ascertain where he came by this document, but we originally used the document with Professor Basara. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, there's another area we haven't discussed yet, and we don't have much time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I may, for the sake of planning the day, how long do you think you will continue your cross-examination; how long does Mr. Pantelic think he will need; and how long will the redirect take?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I need 20 more minutes. I'll try and complete my examination within 20 minutes. Not more than half an hour. I needed two sessions, but I'll do my best and reduce the time. Can Mr. Pantelic say how much time he needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I said - sorry - I cannot but I must --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... whether he will be able to stay within -- fit within that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... to fit myself into this time-frame. We shall finish by the end of this day with Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Redirect included?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only raising this because I've had such difficulty with the times, but Mr. Cvijetic was given 1 hour 30 minutes by Your Honours on the 17th of September, and Mr. Pantelic 1 hour. Mr. Cvijetic is way over the time he was allowed, but that's the situation. Your Honours, as far as re-examination is concerned at the moment I've only got one question, if anything else comes out, there may be more than one, but it's just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: A rough calculation, Mr. Cvijetic, is such that you should wrap up within the next 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we still have an area to cover, and we have to cover it in 20 minutes, as you can see. And it is the attempt on the part of the international community to overcome the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina with a plan which was popularly known as the Cutileiro plan, and so on and to forth. Now, in your report you mention the principles set out in February. However, I have to show you a Defence exhibit, 1D134 is the number, because [indiscernible] negotiations ended by declaring principles adopted on the 18th of March, 1992, at least that is what it says on the document. So would you look at those principles now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There you have them. Yes, document 35, general principles. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of these principles? Have you seen the document before? Do you know about them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the document. I've seen it, although not in a long while.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't go into it in greater detail, we'll leave that to experts in constitutional law. But I'm sure you'll agree with me that that is the document that was signed, or initialled by the parties; right? And that it envisaged a sovereign independent Bosnia and Herzegovina composed of three entities; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly not signed. The Radovan Karadzic made a statement to the Bosnian Serb Assembly shortly after this saying that we would never sign anything that hadn't been agreed to. And the headline in the Sarajevo newspaper "Oslobodenje" said, "Agreed to But Not Signed." So this is, I think, as it states on the very last page, the basis for further negotiations which is the way that the European community spokesman summarised the agreement in a press statement on the 18th, or early on the 19th, after these negotiations were over.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you, Mr. Donia, claim that the agreement, the Lisbon package was signed but that Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his initials from the document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you show me what you are citing?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Let me just take a moment to find it. Yes, here it is. In the B/C/S it is -- well, in English it is pages 29 and 30 of your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The origins of Republika Srpska. And you state there the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic was an unwilling partner in the agreement and withdrew shortly after, et cetera. I apologise for reading that out very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you need to read the full sentence because what was put to him was that he withdrew his initials from the -- what was put to Dr. Donia by Mr. Cvijetic was that he withdrew his initials from the document. That's not what Dr. Donia says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read that paragraph? So what is your answer, did he withdraw his initials or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe, as I said, it's, I think, beyond dispute from the evidence coming from various sources that the document was never signed. Obviously it may have been initialled. I don't know if it was initialled. But initialing a document does not constitute signing it. And certainly, initialing a document that says this will be the basis for further negotiations is, in a sense, not even worth withdrawing from. It was clearly subject to further discussion and agreement, as I state here, particularly on the question of a map. And as you know, those agreements did not take place in the course of subsequent talks. Now, I will say that when Izetbegovic returned in late February, that by a decision of the SDA party counsel, they declined to concur in this agreement, and subsequently Izetbegovic added additional conditions or made specific statements that indicated these talks could not go on in this same spirit this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we just show the video-clip. It's just two minutes long and linked to this particular topic. I'd like to ask our assistant, Ms. Tania, to activate the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take it back to the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I think that this footage denies what you've said, and the authors, Lord Carrington and the rest, claims that it was both signed and that the withdrawal of a signature practically meant war. Do you accept that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- thesis of mine? Not even after you've seen and heard what we have all seen and heard here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of this video-clip, first of all, I think we better identify for the purposes of the record, where it comes from. Second, who it was who was speaking, the man with the moustache at the end, and thirdly, whether the whole video is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, it's my duty to give this information, and that's what Mr. Zecevic has pointed out to me. It is an American-made documentary, it can be found on the internet. So it's a publicly accessible document. It's called the war that could have been avoided. And in this documentary all political and military factors who were active at the time comment the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I showed just an excerpt, but the overall duration is 180 minutes. It's very long. We will probably use other parts of it in the future. So it's a publicly-available document, it can be found on the internet, and I will forward the entire documentary to the OTP because we have it and so they can make use of it as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are we able to identify, please, who the speaker was with the moustache? The young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, whoever we cannot identify, we are trying to establish their identity. Lord Carrington, David Owen, Philippe Morillon feature in that documentary, but we have ourselves been unable to identify all of them. We are working on it, once we bring some of our own expert witnesses, I hope it will be done. But we will let you know as soon as we are done identifying all the persons featuring in that documentary. Your Honours, I don't know whether this video can be admitted; but if not, I move that it be at least marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not even sure about that, because it seems to be we are heading down a side path. This, as I understand the exchange, is a document, albeit in video form, which is in the public domain. The -- you played it and you asked the witness who is on the stand his views on the observation, and he has disagreed, and in the context of this trial, it seems, to me, that is as far as we can take it. To the extent that either side would wish to come back to this for some other purposes, if it is publicly available, then we'd see where we go there. But at this point I don't know that there's anything that could or should be done with this. Certainly not exhibiting it, and I don't even know about marking it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is the Defence are trying to rely on it as evidence of something which is or may be important. In other words, that the Cutileiro plan was actually signed, and then there was a withdrawal by Alija Izetbegovic. Now, there's no dispute of course that Alija Izetbegovic with withdraw, but it's relying on edited -- it's an edit of an edit already made for a film, and I am afraid that real evidence has to be called if this is a point which the defendant has to pursue. They cannot rely on it for the truth of what is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cvijetic, I, for one, have doubts about understanding your point because I don't see the significance of whether or not the Cutileiro plan was signed or just initialled by Mr. Izetbegovic. You referred us just awhile ago to pages 29 and 30 of the witness's report on the origins of the Republika Srpska, and the only thing I can find in the report is on page 30 in the English version where it says that: "The president of the BH Presidency and of the SDA, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, was a reluctant partner in this agreement, and he backed away from the agreement shortly after returning to Sarajevo from Lisbon in late February. But the sticking point proved not to be the principles, but a map." So, Mr. Cvijetic, all I can find on the pages to which you have referred us in the report is the notion that Mr. Izetbegovic backed away from the agreement. And I guess this is undisputed. So where is the importance, or rather, what is the importance of whether or not Mr. Izetbegovic signed it or just initialled it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Furthermore, Mr. Cvijetic, if I may, I don't think I heard one of the officials in this documentary or in this clip, and certainly not Lord Carrington, say or mention that the agreement was signed. The signature of the agreement was only mentioned by the makers of the documentary, not by any one of the officials, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I remember the content well, then it is mentioned that the agreement was signed in Lisbon, and Mr. Zimmerman is quoted as saying that he was a reluctant partner in the negotiations, et cetera, but the essence of our point is that there would have been no war if Mr. Izetbegovic had not withdrawn from the negotiations process. That's our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we should draw a line under this and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I will not deal with the last topic because I have no time for it. You are going into some other historical aspects, notably the Second World War, and our most serious objections are to that.
